explanation: The urinary symptoms, specifically urinary dribbling, are also a direct result of this neurological damage. The bladder's function, particularly its ability to contract and empty, is primarily controlled by the parasympathetic nervous system. Parasympathetic nerve fibers from the sacral spinal cord (S2-S4) stimulate the detrusor muscle of the bladder to contract, allowing for urination. When these parasympathetic pathways are damaged, as they are in tabes dorsalis, the bladder muscle loses its ability to contract effectively. This leads to an overstretched, hypotonic bladder that can't fully empty, resulting in constant overflow and urinary dribbling.

question: A patient came into the eye OPD with complaints of vision loss in both eyes, but he said he can see things from the central part but from both peripheral sides he is unable to see anything. Which of the following is your diagnosis?
explanation: Homonymous hemianopia refers to the loss of vision in the same half of the visual field in both eyes. E.g., a person with a right homonymous hemianopia cannot see anything to the right of the midline in either eye. The question describes a loss on "both peripheral sides," which is a classic presentation of a lesion affecting the optic pathways after the optic chiasm, such as in the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, or occipital cortex.

question: A patient is found to have bilateral homonymous hemianopia. Where is the neurological lesion most likely located?
explanation: Bilateral homonymous hemianopia means the visual pathway is damaged after the crossing point (optic chiasm). The fibers carrying information for one side of the visual field (e.g., the right field) travel together in the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations to the occipital cortex. A lesion in the optic radiation (or the visual cortex itself) on one side will cause the loss of the corresponding visual half in both eyes.

This compression damages the crossing nasal fibers from both eyes resulting in Bitemporal Heminopia.

question: A patient presented with analgesia and thermoanaesthesia of right side of face and weakness of right side of body, where is the disease

options.B: Lateral medullary syndrome of right side

explanation: Medial medullary syndrome: Anterior spinal artery. Pyramid: contralateral spastic paralysis. Medial lemniscus: contralateral loss of tactile, vibration, conscious proprioception. 12th nerve nucleus/fibers: ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of tongue with tongue deviation on protrusion to lesion side. Lateral medullary syndrome: PICA, Wallenberg syndrome. Inferior cerebellar peduncle: ipsilateral limb ataxia. Vestibular nucleus: vertigo, nausea/vomiting, nystagmus (away from lesion). Nucleus ambiguus: ipsilateral paralysis of larynx, pharynx, palate (dysarthria, dysphagia, loss of gag reflex). Spinal V: ipsilateral pain/temperature loss (face). Spinothalamic tract: Contralateral pain and temperature loss (body). Descending hypothalamic: ipsilateral horner syndrome.
